title: Level 3: Seven-Segment Display
aim: To interface a common-cathode 7-segment LED display with the ATmega328P and display the digits 0–9 sequentially using a segment lookup table.
objective: Understand the physical segment layout of a 7-segment display, construct a binary look-up table for each digit, and efficiently write to multiple output pins simultaneously using full-port writes.
theory:
The 7-Segment Display

A 7-segment display is a package of 7 LEDs arranged in the shape of a figure-8, each controlling one segment of the digit. The segments are universally labelled a, b, c, d, e, f, g (plus an optional decimal point dp). By selectively lighting specific combinations of segments, any digit 0–9 (and several letters) can be displayed.

The segment map is:
a = top horizontal, b = top-right vertical, c = bottom-right vertical, d = bottom horizontal, e = bottom-left vertical, f = top-left vertical, g = middle horizontal.

Common-Cathode vs Common-Anode

The two variants share one common pin: Common-Cathode (CC) connects all LED cathodes together to GND, and individual anodes are driven HIGH to light segments. Common-Anode (CA) connects all anodes together to VCC, and individual cathodes are driven LOW to light segments. This experiment uses a common-cathode display — segment ON = corresponding GPIO pin HIGH.

Current Limiting

Each segment LED needs its own current-limiting resistor (typically 220–330 Ω) in series with the GPIO pin. The ATmega328P can source up to 40 mA per pin maximum, but the recommended operating current for a segment is ≈ 10–15 mA for comfortable brightness. Never run all 7 segments without resistors — the cumulative current would exceed safe limits.

Segment Look-Up Table (LUT)

Rather than computing which segments to light on-the-fly, embedded engineers use a look-up table (LUT) — an array indexed by the digit (0–9), where each element is the byte value to write directly to the port. Each bit in the byte corresponds to one segment pin. For example, digit 0 lights segments a,b,c,d,e,f (all except g), so its LUT entry might be 0b00111111 (if segments are wired a→PD0, b→PD1 ... g→PD6).

Efficient Port Writes

Instead of setting individual bits one at a time (7 separate operations per digit), a LUT enables a single-byte write to the entire PORT register: PORTD = segmentLUT[digit];. This updates all 7 segment pins atomically in one instruction — this is critical for displays to avoid visible glitching between segment updates.

Multiplexed Displays

Multi-digit 7-segment displays use multiplexing: all digits share the same segment pins, but each digit has a separate common-enable pin (digit select). By rapidly cycling through digits at > 100 Hz and enabling only one at a time, persistence of vision makes all digits appear simultaneously lit. This experiment uses a single digit for simplicity.

pretest.question: How many segments does a standard 7-segment display have (excluding decimal point)?
pretest.explanation: A 7-segment display has exactly 7 LED segments: a (top), b (top-right), c (bottom-right), d (bottom), e (bottom-left), f (top-left), g (middle).

pretest.question: In a common-cathode 7-segment display, how do you turn ON a segment?
options: Connect VCC to the common pin
pretest.explanation: In common-cathode, all cathodes are tied to GND. Each segment anode must be driven HIGH (+5 V) to forward-bias the LED and turn it on.

pretest.question: Which segments are lit to display the digit '1'?
options: a, b, c, d, e, f
pretest.explanation: The digit '1' uses only the two right-side vertical segments: b (top-right) and c (bottom-right).

pretest.question: What is a Look-Up Table (LUT) in embedded programming?
options: A pre-computed array indexed by input value to retrieve output pattern quickly
pretest.explanation: A LUT is a compile-time array where each index maps to a pre-calculated output bit pattern, enabling O(1) lookup without runtime computation.

pretest.question: Why is a full-port write (PORTD = value) preferable to setting individual bits for a display?
options: All segment pins update simultaneously in one instruction, preventing glitches
pretest.explanation: Sequential bit manipulations create momentary intermediate states visible as display flicker. Writing the whole port at once is atomic and glitch-free.

pretest.question: What current-limiting resistor value is appropriate for a segment driven at 5 V with a 2 V LED forward voltage and 15 mA current?
pretest.explanation: R = (Vsupply − Vf) / If = (5 − 2) / 0.015 = 200 Ω. A 220 Ω standard resistor value works perfectly.

pretest.question: What is the maximum current the ATmega328P can source from a single GPIO pin?
pretest.explanation: The ATmega328P absolute maximum current per I/O pin is 40 mA. Recommended operating current is 20 mA or less for reliability.

pretest.question: What does 0b00111111 represent in a segment byte if bit 0 = segment a, bit 1 = b, ... bit 6 = g?
pretest.explanation: 0b00111111 = bits 0–5 set (a,b,c,d,e,f ON), bit 6 clear (g OFF). This is the pattern for digit '0'.

pretest.question: What technique allows a 4-digit display to share 7 segment pins?
pretest.explanation: Multiplexing rapidly cycles through digits, enabling one digit select pin at a time while updating segment pins. At >100 Hz, persistence of vision makes all digits appear on simultaneously.

pretest.question: Which header provides F_CPU-based delay functions for AVR?
pretest.explanation: <util/delay.h> provides _delay_ms() and _delay_us(), calibrated using the F_CPU macro defined before inclusion.

procedure: Include headers: #include <avr/io.h> and #include <util/delay.h>. Define #define F_CPU 16000000UL. Wire segments a–g to Port D pins PD0–PD6 respectively (each through a 220 Ω resistor). Connect the common cathode to GND.
Configure all of Port D pins 0–6 as outputs: DDRD = 0b01111111;. Bit 7 (PD7) can remain as-is or also be set to output. The value 0x7F sets bits 0–6 as outputs.

Define the 7-segment LUT array for digits 0–9. Each entry encodes which segments are ON (1) or OFF (0): const uint8_t segLUT[10] = {0x3F, 0x06, 0x5B, 0x4F, 0x66, 0x6D, 0x7D, 0x07, 0x7F, 0x6F}; (standard common-cathode encoding where bit 0=a, bit 1=b, ..., bit 6=g).
Create a loop variable: uint8_t digit = 0;. Enter the infinite main loop while(1).
Inside the loop, write the segment pattern for the current digit to Port D: PORTD = segLUT[digit];. This single write atomically updates all 7 segment pins simultaneously.
Wait 1 second so each digit is visible: _delay_ms(1000);.
Increment the digit counter and wrap it: digit = (digit + 1) % 10;. The modulo operation resets to 0 after reaching 9, creating a continuous 0→9→0 cycle.

Verify the display shows each digit for exactly 1 second, cycling 0 through 9 repeatedly. If any segment is missing or extra, check your wiring against the LUT bit assignments and the segment label on the display datasheet.

posttest.question: The LUT value for digit '7' in standard common-cathode encoding is 0x07. Which segments are ON?
posttest.explanation: 0x07 = 0b00000111 = bits 0,1,2 set → segments a, b, c. Digit 7 shows the top horizontal and two right-side verticals.

posttest.question: What is the LUT value for digit '8' (all segments ON)?
posttest.explanation: 0x7F = 0b01111111 = bits 0–6 all set → all 7 segments (a through g) ON. That forms the digit 8.

posttest.question: If you accidentally forget a current-limiting resistor on segment 'a', what happens?
options: Segment 'a' is brighter; over time the LED or GPIO pin may burn out
posttest.explanation: Without a resistor, segment current is limited only by wire resistance — potentially 100+ mA. The LED burns out and the GPIO pin may be damaged beyond the 40 mA max rating.

posttest.question: How would you modify the code to display a digit for only 500 ms instead of 1 second?
posttest.explanation: _delay_ms(500) introduces a 500 ms blocking delay. Since the display period is twice smaller, the cycling rate doubles to 2 digits per second.

posttest.question: What does (digit + 1) % 10 accomplish?
options: Increments digit and resets to 0 after 9
posttest.explanation: The modulo operator (%) returns the remainder of division. (9+1)%10 = 0, providing automatic wrap-around from 9 back to 0.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has Port B, C, and D only. Larger AVR devices (ATmega2560) have Port A.

posttest.question: In a common-anode display, what change would you make to the LUT values?
options: Bitwise invert each value (~0x3F = 0xC0 for digit 0)
posttest.explanation: In common-anode, segments turn ON when driven LOW. So all segment bits are inverted: where CC needs 1 to turn on, CA needs 0.

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM contents on a watchdog reset?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile. Any reset (power-on, watchdog, or external) clears SRAM state — global variables are re-initialized from Flash startup code.

posttest.question: How many bytes of Flash does storing segLUT[10] as a global array consume?
posttest.explanation: Each entry is a uint8_t (1 byte), and there are 10 entries, so the LUT occupies exactly 10 bytes of program Flash.

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: On ISR entry, the AVR hardware clears the I-bit in SREG, preventing nested interrupts. They are restored on RETI.

feedback: Excellent! You've built your first complex output interface — a look-up table driving a multi-LED display. This LUT pattern is fundamental to all display subsystems, from 7-segment to LCD character controllers.
